name: Digital services tax (proposal)
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: impact assessment and third-party estimates; never adopted. Ex-post evidence exists only for national digital services taxes.
summary: Proposed in 2018; stalled in Council, but not listed for withdrawal in the 2027 work programme.

literature.citation: European Commission (2018), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for a Council Directive laying down rules relating to the corporate taxation of a significant digital presence and for a Council Directive on the common system of a digital services tax, SWD(2018) 81 final (executive summary SWD(2018) 82)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals for a Council Directive laying down rules relating to the corporate taxation of a significant digital presence and for a Council Directive on the common system of a digital services tax
literature.outcomes: tax revenues; compliance costs; level playing field
literature.headline: The Commission's assessment of options for taxing the digital economy, covering both the interim digital services tax and the long-term significant digital presence reform.
literature.verified: title and reference checked; full text not read

literature.citation: Copenhagen Economics (2018), The proposed EU digital services tax: Effects on welfare, growth and revenues, study commissioned by CCIA
literature.title: The proposed EU digital services tax: Effects on welfare, growth and revenues
literature.headline: Actual revenues likely well below the Commission's estimate; the impact assessment does not fully consider the distortions and costs for EU consumers and firms.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by CCIA, a tech industry association

literature.citation: Copenhagen Economics (2018), The impact of an EU digital service tax on German businesses, study commissioned by bevh (German e-commerce association)
literature.title: The impact of an EU digital service tax on German businesses
literature.venue: study commissioned by bevh (German e-commerce association)
literature.outcomes: tax incidence; German businesses and consumers
literature.headline: The tax would be passed through at least partly, possibly fully, to German businesses and consumers, partly because of low margins.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by bevh, the German e-commerce association

literature.citation: Klein, Ludwig & Spengel (2019), Ring-fencing Digital Corporations: Investor Reaction to the European Commission's Digital Tax Proposals, ZEW Discussion Paper 19-050 / EconPol Working Paper 36
literature.title: Ring-fencing Digital Corporations: Investor Reaction to the European Commission's Digital Tax Proposals
literature.venue: ZEW Discussion Paper 19-050 / EconPol Working Paper 36
literature.headline: Significant abnormal market reaction of -0.69 percentage points around the release of the draft directives, a loss of at least EUR 52 billion in market value for digital and innovative firms (about 40% US-based); stronger for firms with more profit-shifting potential and EU exposure.

literature.citation: Bauer (2018), Digital Companies and Their Fair Share of Taxes: Myths and Misconceptions, ECIPE Occasional Paper 03/2018
literature.title: Digital Companies and Their Fair Share of Taxes: Myths and Misconceptions
literature.method: descriptive comparison of profit margins and effective tax rates
literature.outcomes: effective tax rates of digital and non-digital firms
literature.headline: Data on profit margins and effective corporate tax rates do not support the claim that digital companies are undertaxed compared with traditional firms.

literature.citation: Langenmayr & Muddasani (2025), Navigating the Amazon: The Incidence of Digital Service Taxes, CESifo Working Paper 12713
literature.title: Navigating the Amazon: The Incidence of Digital Service Taxes
literature.method: empirical analysis of Amazon fee and price data before and after national DSTs
literature.outcomes: platform fees; consumer prices; tax incidence
literature.headline: On national digital services taxes: Amazon raised seller fees by about the tax in France and Spain and by more in the UK, little in Italy, and sellers passed the fees on to consumers, so the taxes fell mainly on consumers.
literature.period_geography: national DSTs in France, Italy, Spain and the UK
